name: libsecp256k1 (bitcoin-core/secp256k1)
workload: ECDSA signature verification (parse compressed pubkey, parse DER signature, verify) on the secp256k1 curve, benchmarked via dlopen loading of historical OpenSSL and libsecp256k1 release versions on the same binary
claimed_speedup: more than 8x faster than OpenSSL's latest release for ECDSA verify (8.5x measured on an AMD Ryzen 5950X, similar ratio on arm64); libsecp256k1 was 2.5-5.5x faster at Bitcoin Core's 2015 switchover from OpenSSL
compiler_and_flags: gcc 14.2.0; default shared-library builds (`./config shared && make` for OpenSSL, default build for libsecp256k1), no special CFLAGS
hardware: arm64 machine (primary run, 3 machines total tested); independently reproduced by libsecp256k1 author Pieter Wuille on an AMD Ryzen 5950X, 500000 iterations
stars_or_usage: 2.5k stars; consensus-critical ECDSA/Schnorr library in Bitcoin Core since 2015, also used by Ethereum, libp2p, and most cryptocurrency software
tradeoffs: Narrow scope (secp256k1 only) vs. OpenSSL's general-purpose EC support; requires a separate dependency instead of reusing an existing OpenSSL install
caveats: Benchmark measures libsecp256k1 built with defaults, not necessarily Bitcoin Core's exact compile flags; author notes OpenSSL has heavily optimized secp256r1 (unlike secp256k1), so the gap is curve-specific, not a general OpenSSL weakness. Older, less rigorous claims of similar magnitude corroborate via the same underlying library: ofek/coincurve's docs ("more than 10x faster than OpenSSL") and piotrnar/gocoin's 2013 changelog ("sipasec cgo ... over 5 times faster than openssl" for EC_Verify).
found_via: GitHub code search: "faster than OpenSSL" ECDSA -> jamesob/delving-bitcoin-archive (mirror of a Nov 2025 delvingbitcoin.org forum post by theStack), reproducible via github.com/theStack/secp256k1-plugbench

name: curve25519-voi
baseline: Go standard library crypto/ed25519 and x/crypto/curve25519 (X25519); also benchmarked against Cloudflare CIRCL
workload: Ed25519 sign/verify/batch-verify (batch sizes 1-1024) and X25519 scalar multiplication
claimed_speedup: Ed25519 Verify ~40% faster than stdlib (125us -> 75us); Sign ~48% faster (52.7us -> 27.5us); VerifyBatch_1024 ~2x faster than stdlib (61.8ms -> 31.7ms, improving to 24.0ms with precomputed public keys); X25519 ScalarBaseMult ~4.5x faster than stdlib (107us -> 24us)
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.17 toolchain, AMD64 with AVX2 assembly backend enabled; also measured with assembly disabled ("purego")
stars_or_usage: 79 stars; used in Oasis Protocol's consensus/runtime stack
tradeoffs: Precomputed public keys cost ~1.47KiB memory each; Go-only, not usable directly from C++; some batch-verify configurations allocate more memory than stdlib
caveats: Baseline is Go's crypto/ed25519 and Cloudflare CIRCL, not OpenSSL/libsodium/BoringSSL/liboqs directly, so baseline_in_list=false; measurements are from a single 2020-era laptop CPU with no libsodium cgo comparison included
found_via: gh api repos/oasisprotocol/curve25519-voi/contents (repo has a dedicated PERFORMANCE.md; found while surveying Ed25519 performance-focused repos)

name: ocaml-curve448
workload: X448 key exchange, Ed448 keypair-from-seed, Ed448 sign and verify of a 64-byte message
claimed_speedup: On AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX PRO 370: C backend Ed448 sign ~2.3x faster than OpenSSL (48us vs 111us), X448 key exchange ~19% faster (93us vs 115us); on Apple M1 Pro sign/key-exchange are roughly on par with OpenSSL; Ed448 verify is consistently slower than OpenSSL (152-203us vs 121-141us) because it is constant-time versus OpenSSL's variable-time double-scalar multiplication
compiler_and_flags: OCaml 5.4.1 / 5.5.1, `dune exec --profile release`; OpenSSL 3.6.4 via `openssl speed`
hardware: Apple M1 Pro (macOS) and AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX PRO 370 (Linux)
tradeoffs: Verification is slower than OpenSSL by design (constant-time vs. OpenSSL's variable-time path); pure-OCaml backend is 2-4x slower than both the C backend and OpenSSL; targets Ed448/X448 rather than the far more common Ed25519/X25519
caveats: Extremely new, zero-star, single-author project; the repo's own docs state "these measurements are recorded results, not a performance guarantee"; the win is workload- and CPU-dependent (a wash on Apple M1, a clear win on the AMD machine) and does not hold for verification
found_via: GitHub code search: "faster than OpenSSL" Ed25519 -> thevilledev/ocaml-curve448 docs/performance.md

name: Go standard library crypto (crypto/ed25519, crypto/ecdsa)
baseline: OpenSSL (via the go-openssl cgo bindings formerly used by go-libp2p)
workload: Signature generation and verification for Ed25519 and ECDSA (non-RSA) node identity keys in the go-libp2p networking stack
claimed_speedup: "The Go standard library is faster than OpenSSL for all key types that are not RSA" (covers Ed25519 and ECDSA sign/verify); RSA verify roughly on par between the two, RSA sign slower in both and worse in the Go stdlib
stars_or_usage: 139k stars; standard library used by nearly all Go programs, including go-libp2p (IPFS, Ethereum consensus clients, Filecoin)
tradeoffs: Go-specific implementations, not usable from C++; go-libp2p dropped its OpenSSL bindings entirely as a result and now depends solely on the stdlib
caveats: No concrete numbers or benchmark methodology published in the CHANGELOG entry itself; it is a first-party engineering decision writeup citing internal profiling rather than a reproducible public benchmark, hence tier C rather than A/B
found_via: GitHub code search: "faster than OpenSSL" Ed25519 -> libp2p/go-libp2p CHANGELOG.md ("Removal of OpenSSL" section)

name: fastcrypto (Secp256k1 FFI backend)
claimed_speedup: ~30% faster verification than the native Rust k256 library, via an FFI wrapper around the C library bitcoin-core/secp256k1
stars_or_usage: 311 stars; production cryptography library for the Sui blockchain
tradeoffs: Depends on a C library via FFI rather than being pure Rust, losing some of k256's memory-safety guarantees and easy portability (e.g. to WASM)
caveats: The ~30% figure is a first-party README claim with no stated methodology, hardware, or reproducible benchmark link; the baseline (k256) is not one of the OpenSSL/libsodium/BoringSSL/liboqs incumbents, though it is the de facto standard pure-Rust secp256k1 implementation, so baseline_in_list is honestly set to false
found_via: gh api repos/MystenLabs/fastcrypto/readme, opened while investigating secp256k1-related speed claims
